"Cells that fire together wire together" is the shortest summary of Hebb's
(1949) rule, and it is a good one. Taken literally, though, the rule has a problem:
nothing in it ever makes a weight smaller. Weights only grow, and they grow
faster the larger they already are. Every textbook on learning spends a
chapter on ways to tame this, and this page shows two of them side by side.

To keep things drawable, the neuron has only two inputs, so its two weights
$w_1$ and $w_2$ form a plane and learning becomes a path through that plane.
Everything runs in your browser. Pick a rule, click anywhere in the plane to
choose a starting point, and watch where the weights go.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = "16px " + getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## The three rules

A single neuron receives two inputs with activities $u_1$ and $u_2$ through
weights $w = (w_1, w_2)$, and its output is $v = w^{\mathsf T} u$. The basic
Hebbian rule says that each weight changes in proportion to the product of
its input and the output, $\tau\, dw/dt = v\,u$. We are not interested in the
jittery response to individual input patterns, only in the average drift of
the weights over many patterns. Averaging replaces $v\,u$ by $Q\,w$, where
$Q = \langle u u^{\mathsf T} \rangle$ is the correlation matrix of the inputs.
For two inputs of equal strength it is

$$Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & q \\ q & 1 \end{pmatrix},$$

and the single number $q$, the correlation between the two inputs, is the
slider you will use most. Positive $q$ means the inputs tend to be active
together, negative $q$ means that one is active when the other is quiet. The
three rules are then

$$\text{Hebbian:}\quad \tau \frac{dw}{dt} = Q\,w$$

$$\text{with bounds:}\quad \tau \frac{dw}{dt} = Q\,w, \qquad 0 \le w_i \le 1$$

$$\text{Oja:}\quad \tau \frac{dw}{dt} = Q\,w - \alpha\,(w^{\mathsf T} Q\, w)\,w .$$

The first is Hebb's rule as it stands. The second is the same rule with a
fence around it: each weight is clipped to the interval $[0, 1]$, which is
the simplest thing an implementation can do and roughly what a synapse that
cannot become negative or arbitrarily strong would do. The third is Oja's
(1982) rule, which subtracts a term proportional to the output's variance
times the weight itself. The subtracted term grows faster than the Hebbian term, so it
acts as a brake that kicks in once the weights are large. The parameter
$\alpha$ sets how hard the brake is, and $\tau$ only sets the overall speed.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof hbRule = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Hebbian", "hebb"], ["Hebbian with bounds [0, 1]", "bounded"], ["Oja's rule", "oja"]]), {value: "hebb", label: "Rule"})
viewof hbQ = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: -0.4, step: 0.05, label: "Input correlation q"})
viewof hbAlpha = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Oja α (Oja's rule only)"})
viewof hbPause = Inputs.toggle({label: "Pause"})
viewof hbReplay = Inputs.button("Replay")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
hbCol = ({C0: "#1f77b4", C1: "#ff7f0e", C2: "#2ca02c", K: "#444", T1: "#9467bd", T2: "#17becf"})
hbLay = ({W: 760, H: 400, S: 340, m: 80, top: 16})   // plane occupies x in [m, m+S], y in [top, top+S]
mutable hbClick = null
hbCanvas = {
  const c = mkCanvas(hbLay.W, hbLay.H);
  c.canvas.style.cursor = "crosshair";
  c.canvas.addEventListener("click", ev => {
    const r = c.canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
    const x = (ev.clientX - r.left) * hbLay.W / r.width, y = (ev.clientY - r.top) * hbLay.H / r.height;
    const {m, S, top} = hbLay;
    if (x < m || x > m + S || y < top || y > top + S) return;
    mutable hbClick = {fx: (x - m) / S, fy: 1 - (y - top) / S};
  });
  return c;
}
hbLimits = ({hebb: [-2, 2], bounded: [-0.1, 1.1], oja: [-1.2, 1.2]})
hbStart = {
  const [lo, hi] = hbLimits[hbRule];
  if (!hbClick) return [0.01, 0.05];
  return [lo + (hi - lo) * hbClick.fx, lo + (hi - lo) * hbClick.fy];
}
hbStep = (w, rule, q, alpha, dt = 0.1) => {
  const Qw = [w[0] + q * w[1], q * w[0] + w[1]];
  let n;
  if (rule === "oja") { const wQw = w[0] * Qw[0] + w[1] * Qw[1];
    n = [w[0] + dt * (Qw[0] - alpha * wQw * w[0]), w[1] + dt * (Qw[1] - alpha * wQw * w[1])]; }
  else n = [w[0] + dt * Qw[0], w[1] + dt * Qw[1]];
  if (rule === "bounded") n = [Math.min(1, Math.max(0, n[0])), Math.min(1, Math.max(0, n[1]))];
  return n;
}
hbEndColour = (w, rule) => {
  const near = (a, b, tol) => Math.abs(w[0] - a) < tol && Math.abs(w[1] - b) < tol;
  if (rule === "bounded") { if (near(1, 1, 1e-3)) return hbCol.C0; if (near(0, 1, 1e-3)) return hbCol.C1; if (near(1, 0, 1e-3)) return hbCol.C2; }
  if (rule === "oja") { const r = Math.SQRT1_2; if (near(r, r, 0.02)) return hbCol.C0; if (near(-r, r, 0.02)) return hbCol.C1; if (near(r, -r, 0.02)) return hbCol.C2; }
  return hbCol.K;
}
hbField = {
  const N = 20, steps = 100, trajs = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) for (let j = 0; j < N; j++) {
    let w = [i / (N - 1), j / (N - 1)]; const pts = [w];
    for (let s = 0; s < steps; s++) { w = hbStep(w, hbRule, hbQ, hbAlpha); pts.push(w); }
    trajs.push({pts, col: hbEndColour(w, hbRule)});
  }
  return trajs;
}
hbTraj = {
  hbReplay;
  const steps = 100; let w = hbStart; const pts = [w]; let k = 0;
  while (true) {
    if (!viewof hbPause.value && k < steps) { w = hbStep(w, hbRule, hbQ, hbAlpha); pts.push(w); k++; }
    yield {pts, done: k >= steps, col: k >= steps ? hbEndColour(w, hbRule) : hbCol.K};
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const c = hbCanvas, fg = exFg(), {W, H, S, m, top} = hbLay;
  const [lo, hi] = hbLimits[hbRule];
  const px = w => m + S * (w - lo) / (hi - lo), py = w => top + S * (1 - (w - lo) / (hi - lo));
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  axisBox(c, m, top, S, S);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText("w₁", m + S / 2, top + S + 24); c.fillText(lo, px(lo), top + S + 24); c.fillText(hi, px(hi), top + S + 24);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("w₂", m - 10, top + S / 2 + 5); c.fillText(lo, m - 8, py(lo) + 5); c.fillText(hi, m - 8, py(hi) + 5);
  c.save(); c.beginPath(); c.rect(m, top, S, S); c.clip();
  c.lineWidth = 1;
  for (const {pts, col} of hbField) {
    c.strokeStyle = col; c.globalAlpha = 0.25; c.beginPath();
    pts.forEach((p, i) => i ? c.lineTo(px(p[0]), py(p[1])) : c.moveTo(px(p[0]), py(p[1]))); c.stroke();
  }
  c.globalAlpha = 1; c.lineWidth = 2.5; c.strokeStyle = hbTraj.col; c.beginPath();
  hbTraj.pts.forEach((p, i) => i ? c.lineTo(px(p[0]), py(p[1])) : c.moveTo(px(p[0]), py(p[1]))); c.stroke();
  const last = hbTraj.pts[hbTraj.pts.length - 1], first = hbTraj.pts[0];
  c.fillStyle = hbTraj.col; c.beginPath(); c.arc(px(last[0]), py(last[1]), 6, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill();
  c.strokeStyle = fg; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.beginPath(); c.arc(px(first[0]), py(first[1]), 6, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.stroke();
  c.restore();
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText(`start (${first[0].toFixed(2)}, ${first[1].toFixed(2)}) · click to move`, m + 8, top + 22);
  // time course, right
  const x0 = m + S + 70, tW = W - x0 - 16;
  const tx = i => x0 + tW * i / 100, ty = w => py(w);
  axisBox(c, x0, top, tW, S);
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("time steps", x0 + tW / 2, top + S + 24);
  c.fillText("0", tx(0), top + S + 24); c.fillText("100", tx(100), top + S + 24);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText(lo, x0 - 8, py(lo) + 5); c.fillText(hi, x0 - 8, py(hi) + 5);
  c.save(); c.beginPath(); c.rect(x0, top, tW, S); c.clip();
  for (const [j, col] of [[0, hbCol.T1], [1, hbCol.T2]]) {
    c.strokeStyle = col; c.lineWidth = 2; c.beginPath();
    hbTraj.pts.forEach((p, i) => i ? c.lineTo(tx(i), ty(p[j])) : c.moveTo(tx(i), ty(p[j]))); c.stroke();
  }
  c.restore();
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillStyle = hbCol.T1; c.fillText("w₁", x0 + 8, top + 22); c.fillStyle = hbCol.T2; c.fillText("w₂", x0 + 44, top + 22);
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

The square on the left is the weight plane, $w_1$ along the bottom and $w_2$
up the side. The thick line is the trajectory from your starting point, which
is marked by the open circle. It ends at the filled dot. Behind it, the faint
lines are trajectories started from a grid of points, so you can see the
overall flow of the rule at a glance. All of these are coloured by where they
end up after 100 steps. For the bounded rule, blue means both weights
saturated at 1, orange means $(0, 1)$ and green means $(1, 0)$. For Oja's
rule the end points are unit vectors instead, blue for $(1,1)/\sqrt2$, orange
for $(-1,1)/\sqrt2$ and green for $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$. Grey means none of the
above. Plain Hebbian learning is grey everywhere, since nothing ever stops.

The panel on the right shows the same trajectory as two curves against time,
$w_1$ in purple and $w_2$ in teal. It is easier to see from this panel
whether a weight has settled or is still moving.

## Things to try

Begin with the plain Hebbian rule and the default negative correlation. From
any starting point the weights head off along a diagonal and leave the plot.
Which diagonal depends on $q$: the weights grow fastest along the eigenvector
of $Q$ with the largest eigenvalue, and that is $(1, 1)$ when the inputs are
positively correlated and $(1, -1)$ when they are anticorrelated. Move $q$
through zero and watch the flow swing from one diagonal to the other. At
$q = 0$ both eigenvalues are equal and every direction grows at the same
rate, so the trajectories are straight rays from the origin.

Switch to the bounded rule. The runaway is gone, but something else has
appeared: the plane is divided into regions, each draining into a different
corner. A starting point that favours input 1 ends at $(1, 0)$, one that
favours input 2 at $(0, 1)$, and with positive correlation most of the plane
ends at $(1, 1)$. These regions are the basins of attraction of the three
stable corners, and the bounds have turned a rule with no stable state into
one that stores a decision about which input wins. Change $q$ and watch the
boundaries between the basins move.

Switch to Oja's rule. Now the trajectories bend towards a circle of radius
$1/\sqrt{\alpha}$ and then slide along it to an eigenvector of $Q$. The rule
does two things at once: it normalises the weight vector and it picks out the
direction of largest input variance, which is the first principal component
of the inputs. That is not a coincidence, it is the main reason Oja's rule is
famous. Raise $\alpha$ and the circle shrinks. Set $q$ to zero and the
trajectories still reach the circle, but stop wherever they land on it,
since no direction is preferred.

This page is based on the Hebbian learning exercise in Dayan and Abbott
(2001, chapter 8). Miller and MacKay (1994) give a careful comparison of
different ways of constraining Hebbian learning, including why subtractive
and multiplicative normalisation lead to different outcomes, which is
exactly the difference between the bounded rule and Oja's rule above.

## References

Dayan P, Abbott LF (2001). *Theoretical Neuroscience: Computational and
Mathematical Modeling of Neural Systems*. MIT Press.

Hebb DO (1949). *The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory*.
Wiley.

Miller KD, MacKay DJC (1994). The role of constraints in Hebbian learning.
*Neural Computation* 6: 100–126.

Oja E (1982). A simplified neuron model as a principal component analyzer.
*Journal of Mathematical Biology* 15: 267–273.
